blocks.x: Contracts that pass independent audits at zero highs: formal-verified cores with invariant coverage measured, fuzzing that runs around the clock, upgrade discipline that removes ambush risk — and a spec written before the first line of Solidity.
The specification is the contract — the code is its executable form
blocks.sub: Spec-first engineering with proofs, fuzzing and governed upgrades

blocks.x: Smart contracts are business law in executable form — and like law, the writing matters more than the cleverness. The practice is boring on purpose: minimal contract surfaces, formal verification of the core, independent audits with zero high-severity findings, and upgrade mechanisms (proxies, governance) that are themselves audited.

The lifecycle is the discipline: spec first, audit before deploy, staged rollout with monitoring, and an incident path rehearsed like any production system — because a contract bug is a business-logic bug with finality.
Below: the failure modes that put vulnerabilities on mainnet, the reference architecture of the verification pipeline, and the console that tracks audit readiness.

widgets.title: The assurance pipeline — click stages for the gate

stages.name: Spec
stages.detail: State invariants and trust model written before code; every invariant is an executable property the fuzzer will attack for the rest of the project.

stages.name: Build
stages.detail: Implementation against spec with the fuzz harness in CI — violations block merges, and every fix strengthens a property rather than patching a symptom.

stages.name: Review
stages.detail: Internal review runs adversarial passes (economic exploits, griefing, oracle windows) with findings filed against invariants — the list auditors later see is short by design.

stages.name: Audit
stages.detail: External audit with the spec attached; findings triaged with the same invariant discipline, and the audit report becomes part of the deploy evidence.

stages.name: Deploy
stages.detail: Deployment via key ceremony with timelock and pause authority defined; post-deploy monitoring watches invariant proxies on mainnet state.

widgets.note: The pipeline's point: auditors confirm, they do not discover — the classes they find were excluded by construction.

Invariants are written before code exists
blocks.sub: Spec-first engineering — formal verification, fuzzing, audits and the upgrade discipline

blocks.x: Contract failures are specification failures that shipped: the code does faithfully what nobody wrote down. The discipline inverts the order — the executable specification states the invariants (what must always be true), the business rules and the failure paths, and stakeholders sign it before implementation begins. Formal verification then proves the invariants hold on the contract, property-based fuzzing attacks the boundaries the proofs assume, and the independent audit is scoped against the spec so findings map to named invariants rather than generic concern lists.

Deployment is not the end of the engineering: runtime monitors check the invariants live (a violated invariant pages before funds move), and upgrade governance is multi-sig with timelock and notice — the change window is a governed event with a rollback plan, not a deploy button. The console reads invariant coverage, monitor violations and audit remediation state, because a contract estate whose safety posture is a PDF is a liability wearing a badge.

items: Invariants and failure paths signed by stakeholders before implementation.
Formal verification plus fuzzing on the boundaries proofs assume.

Violations page before funds move; upgrades timelocked and noticed.
What does "zero highs" actually mean for an audit?

Independent audits return zero high-severity findings because the invariants were specified and formally checked before code existed — the audit verifies the spec rather than discovering it. The console tracks invariant coverage per contract layer.
How do you handle upgrades to deployed contracts?

Upgrade governance is part of the contract: proxy patterns are chosen against the charter, upgrade paths are gated, and the overlay records who can trigger what. The upgrade-bug class is closed by design, not by hope.
Which parts get formal verification, and which do not?

Coverage follows money and trust: core ledger at 95%, token logic at 90%, access control at 92% — while view helpers at 30% are covered by tests. The defaults table names where proof stops and the deviation it would need.
Can you work with our existing contracts and oracles?

Yes — the integration surface names ledgers, oracles and business systems. Existing contracts enter through the same gates: spec recovery, invariant capture and an audit-readiness read before any change ships.
What does the engineering team inherit?
The spec corpus, invariant suite, test harness, audit reports and the console — plus the change discipline: spec diff to audited release is a repeatable path, not a heroic one.
